papers.title: Programmed Cell Death-1 marks TOX+ T Regulatory Cells that Inhibit Autoimmunity and Anti-Tumor Immunity
papers.abstract: Regulatory T cells (Tregs) are important for the maintenance of immune homeostasis. A proportion of peripheral Tregs constitutively express the coreceptor programmed cell death-1 (PD1), but the importance of this subset is yet to be investigated. We found PD1 marks TOX expressing Tregs. In both PD1 germline deficient and peripheral deficient Tregs, an increase in TOX+ Tregs were noted in steady state which was reproduced in antibody-based blocking studies. We next investigated if TOX+ Tregs were present in disease states. For this we utilised an experimental murine model of melanoma, colorectal cancer and autoimmune colitis. In all experimental conditions, TOX+ Tregs were present and marked by PD-1. To explore the function of PD1+TOX+ Tregs, we utilised a PD1-DTR switch. We found deleting PD1+ Tregs that marked TOX abrogated tumor suppression and enhanced T cell mediated colitis. Mechanistically, we found PD1+TOX+ Treg inhibited the functional plasticity of PD1-Tregs. Taken together, this study identifies PD1 and TOX as markers of Treg function and highlights potential new immunotherapeutic approaches such as PD1+Treg cell depletion for enhanced anti-tumor responses.

papers.title: A cross-species single-cell spatial atlas of kidney allografts
papers.abstract: Kidney allografts with the same Banff diagnosis differ in their immune microenvironments and functional recovery after treatment, yet the tissue features distinguishing recovery from non-recovery remain unclear. We constructed SPECTRA (Spatial Etiology and Coordination of Transplant Rejection in Allografts), which comprises spatial multi-omic data from 1,011,984 cells in 83 human allograft biopsies. We also profiled 442,320 cells from 34 mouse grafts across experimental groups and time points by single-cell sequencing, and integrated a public human single-cell reference of 352,911 cells. Unsupervised analysis identified nine tissue niches, of which plasma-cell effector niche occupancy was associated with less eGFR improvement approximately 90 days after biopsy ({rho} = -0.508, q = 0.0165). Plasma cells in this niche expressed IGHG1, IGKC and TXNDC5; in scarred interstitium, plasma-cell XBP1, HSPA5 and SEC61A1 expression increased with fibrosis. Tertiary lymphoid structures retained TCF7-high stem-like T cells that received CCL19-CCR7 signals from fibroblasts. Using multimodal deep-learning models to delineate anatomical regions, we separated Banff lesions into local immune-load and chronic morphological-injury axes, each with distinct compartmental responses. Peritubular-capillary endothelium increased interferon-{gamma}-associated antigen presentation with local immune load, glomerular endothelium reduced MHC expression with glomerular inflammation, and chronic injury was accompanied by reduced metabolic programmes in specific cell types. In mice, we built a single-cell atlas of kidney transplantation covering syngeneic grafts and BALB/c, DBA/2J and DBA/2N[->]C57BL/6 models. Graft trajectories separated into rejection-associated and tolerance-associated paths that differed in interferon-activated myeloid states and Hnf4a- and Ppara-associated tubular metabolism. In 20 human recipients with rejection-spectrum diagnoses, predictions of functional non-response from a hierarchical causal-inference model were most sensitive to plasma-cell niche occupancy and density. Niche maps predicted from routine H&E were associated with subsequent kidney function. These findings show that kidney allograft rejection is accompanied by changes in cellular states and spatial organisation, and identify plasma-cell niches in residual and scarred interstitium as tissue features of functional non-recovery after rejection.

papers.title: Integrated multi-omics framework mapping Myeloid associated cellular states (M.A.C.S.)
papers.abstract: Functional specialization of myeloid cells in vivo aligns poorly with historic binary classifications. Moreover, inconsistent annotations hinder comparisons across studies. Here, we present Myeloid Associated Cell States (M.A.C.S.), an integrated multiomics framework combining a human Myeloid Cell Atlas (MCA) comprising 498,642 cells from 581 donors across 7 tissues in health and disease with probabilistic mapping of cell populations. Batch-aware variable gene selection preserves tissue-imprinted and disease-associated programs, resolving 24 core states with consensus gene signatures. We introduce scLAVI to quantify population-level similarity with gene-level attribution. These tools resolve resident macrophages into 13 distinct states defined by a combination of a core residence program and tissue-specific programs that are altered upon disease and identify lipid- and scar-associated macrophages as distinct states with complementary roles. M.A.C.S. enables systematic comparison of myeloid cell states across tissues, diseases and experimental activation models, connecting controlled perturbations in vitro to functional specialization in vivo.

papers.title: Agonistic anti-CD40 monoclonal antibody improves the antitumor efficacy of a clinical chemo-immunotherapy regimen in a refractory mouse neuroblastoma model.
papers.abstract: Background: The current standard regimen for relapsed-refractory high-risk neuroblastoma (HR-NB) is the combination of chemotherapy agents -Temozolomide and Irinotecan - and anti-GD2 antibody dinutuximab (TIG). This treatment results in an overall response for ~40% of patients, but the remaining 60% are resistant to TIG. We hypothesized that agonistic anti-CD40 monoclonal antibody (aCD40), which activates antitumor NK cells and macrophages as we found in previous studies, will improve the efficacy of TIG. Aim: To test the combination of aCD40 and TIG in a mouse HR-NB model that is resistant to TIG. Methods: For these studies, we used a clinically relevant, immunologically cold, HR-NB murine model, 9464D-GD2. Syngeneic mice were intradermally injected with the tumor cells. When tumors were established, mice were randomized and treated with TIG and/or aCD40. Tumor growth and mouse survival were followed. Mice that rejected their tumors were rechallenged to test immunological memory. Changes in immune cells were evaluated by flow cytometry and single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNAseq). Results: Similar to ~60% of patients with relapsed/refractory HR-NB, mice bearing 9464D-GD2 tumors did not respond to TIG. Adding aCD40 to TIG induced complete tumor regression in most mice bearing small tumors and extended survival, with many mice remaining tumor-free. The combination of aCD40 and TIG was more effective than aCD40 alone. The antitumor effect of TIG+aCD40 was not inhibited in T cell- or neutrophil-depleted mice but was substantially reduced in NK cell- and macrophage-depleted mice, indicating a role for both NK cells and macrophages in the antitumor effect. Involvement of these cells was consistent with flow cytometry and scRNAseq analyses. Mice treated with TIG+aCD40 that remained tumor-free were rechallenged with 9464D-GD2 cells and showed significantly reduced tumor growth compared to naive mice, indicating a memory response. This memory response was reduced in T cell-depleted mice, indicating the involvement of T cells in memory. Conclusion: These results show that while TIG alone was ineffective, a combination of aCD40 and TIG induced substantial tumor eradication in the 9464D-GD2 tumor model, suggesting that aCD40 may warrant future testing as an addition to the current standard TIG regimen for children with relapsed-refractory HR-NB.

papers.title: Mucosal B Cell Aggregates are Associated with Non-response to JAK1 Inhibitor Therapy in Ulcerative Colitis
papers.abstract: Ulcerative colitis (UC) is a chronic inflammatory bowel disease with considerable interindividual variation in treatment response and limited efficacy of available therapies in some patients. Predicting individual responses is therefore essential for personalized treatment selection. Filgotinib, a preferential JAK1 inhibitor, induces clinical remission in approximately 40% of patients after 1 year, but mechanisms underlying response remain unclear. Using 38-marker imaging mass cytometry, and immunohistochemistry, we profiled paired colonic biopsies from 25 UC patients before and during filgotinib treatment. Full response (n=8) was defined as an endoscopic Mayo score of 0 at the biopsy site after ten weeks of treatment, while non-response (n=6) was defined as no score improvement at the biopsy site. At baseline, despite comparable inflammation and JAK/STAT activity, full responders showed greater epithelial abundance, whereas non-responders had more B cells. In non-responders, B cells were also more frequently organized into lymphoid aggregates containing ICOS+ CD4 memory and CD57+ CD8 memory T cells. Abundance of these B cell-rich aggregates correlated negatively with lamina propria pJAK1 abundance. This suggests that inflammation driven by these lymphoid aggregates may be relatively JAK1-independent and could therefore contribute to filgotinib non-response. After 10 weeks, neutrophils and HLA-DR+ epithelial cells had decreased more in full responders than in non-responders. These findings suggest that baseline mucosal cell composition and organization differ between future responders and non-responders, and that filgotinib normalizes mucosal immune cell abundances in full responders. These cellular subsets warrant further investigation for their potential relevance to treatment stratification and pharmacodynamic monitoring of JAK-targeted therapy.

papers.title: Dual-loop DogTag engineering enables modular antigen display on human vault nanoparticles
papers.abstract: Self-assembling protein nanoparticles can enhance immune responses by displaying multiple copies of an antigen on their surface. Most previous studies using vault nanoparticles have focused on loading proteins inside the particle or modifying its ends. Here, we introduced two DogTag peptides into separate surface-exposed loops of human major vault protein (MVP), creating up to 156 potential attachment sites on each 78-subunit vault. The engineered MVP formed vault-sized particles in suspension HEK cells, to which separately produced, stabilized influenza H5N1 Clade 2.3.4.4b hemagglutinin (HA) fused to DogCatcher was covalently attached. By varying the amount of HA added, we obtained preparations with estimated loadings of approximately 32, 64, and 124 HA trimers per vault. Structural models showed that increasing HA loading reduced the median distance between neighboring HA trimers from 13.3 to 8.8 nm, while electron microscopy showed that highly loaded particles retained their characteristic vault morphology. Following subcutaneous priming and intranasal boosting in mice, highly loaded HA-decorated vaults induced significantly higher HA-specific serum IgG, IgG1, IgG2a, and IgA titers than soluble HA. Covalent attachment of HA to vaults also resulted in significantly higher IgG2a titers than the non-conjugated mixture of vaults and HA, reaching levels similar to those induced by CpG-adjuvanted HA. Despite the strong HA-specific antibody responses, anti-vault IgG titers remained low. Our approach adds high-density, adjustable antigen display to the established cargo-loading and targeting capabilities of human vaults, offering the possibility of combining all three functions in a single vaccine particle.

papers.title: Complex IV Subunit C15orf48 Integrates Electron Transport Chain Function with Amino Acid and Lipid Metabolism to Regulate Innate Immunity
papers.abstract: Despite extensive recognition of immunometabolism in innate immune regulation, how mitochondrial bioenergetic and metabolic pathways in monocytes interface to control inflammatory responses remains poorly understood. Here, we uncover that C15orf48 (MOCCI/NMES1/COXFA4L3), an inflammation-associated mitochondrial complex IV (CIV) subunit, orchestrates electron transport chain (ETC) function, fatty acid oxidation (FAO), and branched-chain amino acid (BCAA) catabolism to control monocyte activation. Loss of C15orf48 globally and in monocytes confers host tolerance and resistance to bacterial pneumonia and LPS-induced endotoxemia, characterized by reduced inflammatory gene expression, cytokine secretion, and monocyte activation. Mechanistically, C15orf48 increases mitochondrial ROS production and maintains NAD pools, which in turn supports long-chain FAO and BCAA catabolism required for robust monocyte activation and inflammatory cytokine production. These findings define a mitochondrial CIV metabolic axis directed by C15orf48 as central to monocyte activation and innate immunity, filling a key knowledge gap in immunometabolic control and presenting new targets for therapy in infection and sepsis.

papers.title: Whole-blood and PBMC-based assays reveal hidden inflammatory responses to decellularized materials for heart valve replacement
papers.abstract: Reliable assessment of inflammatory activity is essential for the development of biological heart valve materials. However, the responses detected depend critically on the assay system. Following inconsistent and weak responses in standard macrophage assays, we systematically compared human whole blood with isolated immune-cell models to evaluate laboratory-prepared decellularized aortic valves from human donors and clinically used biological valve materials. The laboratory-prepared valves underwent histological and biochemical characterization and were prepared using the same protocol used for ovine aortic valves transplanted in vivo. They induced pronounced proinflammatory responses in whole blood and peripheral blood mononuclear cells (PBMCs) compared with clinical valve prostheses, whereas macrophages and THP-1 cells showed little cytokine release for any of the materials. Surface coating was associated with lower levels of selected cytokines but did not eliminate inflammatory activity. PBMCs readily detected proinflammatory activity, while whole blood revealed additional response patterns. In whole blood, fixed bovine and porcine pericardium induced higher expression of selected proinflammatory genes than decellularized human aortic valve tissue. Median IFN-2 concentrations were highest with the human valve tissue. These findings demonstrate that material characterization does not replace functional assessment of inflammatory activity and that assay selection determines which aspects of the response are captured. PBMC and whole-blood testing provide complementary functional approaches for comparing material preparations. Together, these assays support the evaluation of tissue processing and surface modification in biological heart valve development.

papers.title: Human Lung Mast cell Diversity Across Anatomical Compartments Defined by Single-Cell Transcriptomics
papers.abstract: Background: Mast cells are key regulators of inflammatory lung diseases, including asthma. Yet, the heterogeneity of lung mast cells and their specialization in different lung compartments remain poorly defined. Traditional protease-based classifications fail to capture distinct mast cell states relevant to airway pathology, highlighting the need for high-resolution, compartment-resolved analyses. Objective: To determine the heterogeneity of human lung mast cells in different lung compartments. Methods: We performed single-cell RNA sequencing analysis of human lung mast cells from four anatomical compartments; bronchi, parenchyma, arteries and veins. Bioinformatical analysis was used to characterize mast cell heterogeneity and compartment-specific specialization. Results: Five transcriptional distinct mast cell states (MC1-MC5) were identified. MC1 was characterized by stress response (e.g., MT2A, MRPL14, SNN), MC2 by broad immediate-early gene activation (e.g., FOS, JUN), and MC3 by a more selective activation with TGF-{beta} response enrichment. MC4 displayed a pro-inflammatory effector phenotype enriched for IL-33-responses (e.g., CCL2, CCL4, CCL4L2, IL13), consistent with roles in airway inflammation. MC5 was associated with long non-coding RNAs (MEG3, MEG8). Mast cell states showed anatomical segregation with inflammatory cytokines enriched in bronchial and arterial mast cells while reduced in parenchymal mast cells. We further identified MCTC-like mast cells co-expressing CTSG, CMA1 and ADCYAP1, characterized by enhanced metabolic programming. Conclusions: This study provides a comprehensive single-cell transcriptomic atlas of human lung mast cells, revealing five distinct transcriptional states and compartment-specific functional specialization. These findings link mast cell heterogeneity to airway inflammation and provide a translational framework for targeting mast cells in lung diseases.

papers.title: A modular intranasal Nm-nOMV RBD concatemer vaccine induces broad betacoronavirus-neutralizing antibodies
authors: W. J. P. van den Braak
papers.abstract: Betacoronaviruses pose a major threat to human and animal health due to their propensity to cause spillover infections. Broadly protective vaccines that induce mucosal immunity may strengthen pandemic preparedness by limiting infection and onward transmission. Here we have developed intranasal betacoronavirus vaccine candidates combining AdJane Biosciences' Neisseria meningitidis native outer membrane vesicle (Nm-nOMV) platform, a self-adjuvating mucosal delivery platform recently shown to be safe and well tolerated in a first-in-human Phase 1 trial, with multivalent coronavirus spike immunogens. We evaluated betacoronaviruses full Spike proteins, chimeric full Spike proteins, and Receptor Binding Domain (RBD) concatemers representing sarbecoviruses, merbecoviruses, and embecoviruses. Antigenic profiling identified immunogens retaining activity against human convalescent sera and characterized monoclonal antibodies. In mice, intranasal immunization with Nm-nOMVs combined with RBD concatemers induced mucosal IgA responses, systemic IgG and broad neutralization of homologous and heterologous human and bat related betacoronaviruses. Together, findings from the study identify multivalent RBD concatemers co-administered with the Nm-nOMV platform as a promising, modular antigen design for the development of broadly protective mucosal vaccines against emerging betacoronaviruses.

papers.title: The unfolded protein response in alveolar type II cells is a therapeutic target in ischemia-reperfusion injury and chronic lung allograft rejection
papers.abstract: Although lung transplantation is life saving for patients with end-stage lung disease, its long-term outcome is poor owing to an inexorable process of chronic rejection that culminates in chronic lung allograft dysfunction (CLAD) and death or the need for re-transplantation at a median of 6 years post-transplant. Current immunosuppression fails to prevent CLAD, suggesting the existence of alternative pathways not susceptible to these drugs. Lung-directed autoantibodies have been shown to predict CLAD and reduced post-transplant survival. Here, we observed that serum and bronchoalveolar lavage antibodies to GRP78, a master regulator of the unfolded protein response, identified patients at increased risk for CLAD and death. Anti-GRP78 antibodies were associated with upregulation of HSPA5, the gene encoding GRP78, in alveolar type II cells from human lung allografts, and with translocation of GRP78 to the cell surface, a hallmark of the unfolded protein response. Cell surface GRP78 expression was triggered by lung ischemia-reperfusion injury and was also prominent during the development of ischemia-reperfusion injury-augmented chronic rejection in a mouse lung transplant model. Treatment with the chemical chaperones 4-PBA and TUDCA, which are known to ameliorate endoplasmic reticulum stress during the unfolded protein response, reduced both ischemia-reperfusion injury and chronic allograft rejection in vitro and in mice. Taken together, our data implicate alveolar type II cell stress in the pathogenesis of lung ischemia-reperfusion injury and fibrotic chronic lung allograft rejection and suggest that this phenomenon can be targeted for clinical benefit.

papers.title: Angiostrongylus cantonensis fifth-stage larvae Excretory-Secretory Products Induce Presenilin-1-Associated Molecular Changes and Inflammatory Responses in Mouse Astrocytes
papers.abstract: Background Parasite infection may cause significant effects on the immune response in the host brain. Previous studies have demonstrated that excretory-secretory products (ESPs) released by fifth-stage larvae (L5) of Angiostrongylus cantonensis induce inflammatory responses in mouse astrocytes. However, the underlying molecular mechanisms involved in ESP-induced neuroinflammation remain unclear. Therefore, this study aimed to investigate the molecular mechanisms underlying inflammatory responses in mouse astrocytes following treatment with A. cantonensis L5 ESPs. Methods Mouse astrocytes were treated with A. cantonensis L5 ESPs to investigate changes in the JNK-related inflammatory signaling pathway, including Presenilin-1 (PS1), glycogen synthase kinase-3{beta} (GSK-3{beta}), {beta}-catenin, nuclear factor kappa B (NF-{kappa}B), and interleukin-6 (IL-6). Furthermore, the JNK inhibitor - SP600125 was also employed to determine the mechanism between JNK pathway and inflammation induced by A. cantonensis L5 ESPs. Results Treatment with A. cantonensis L5 ESPs showed a significant increase tenses in PS1, GSK-3{beta}, NF-{kappa}B, and IL-6, while the expression of {beta}-catenin decreased during post 12 until 24 hours treatment. Furthermore, pretreatment with SP600125 attenuated ESP-induced PS1 and GSK-3{beta} expression, which restored {beta}-catenin expression. These findings suggest that JNK-associated signaling helps regulate PS1-associated molecular responses and inflammatory signaling in astrocytes exposed to A. cantonensis L5 ESPs. Conclusions A. cantonensis L5 ESPs induce an inflammatory response in mouse astrocytes, which is accompanied by JNK-related and GSK-{beta}/{beta}-catenin signaling pathways. Inhibition of JNK signaling attenuates these molecular changes, suggesting that JNK-associated signaling may contribute to parasite-derived ESP-induced inflammation. These findings provide further insight into the molecular interactions between A. cantonensis and host astrocytes.

papers.title: CD33-CAR iNKT cells overcome acute myeloid leukemia heterogeneity by activating CD8+ T cells and enhancing tumor immunogenicity
papers.abstract: Acute myeloid leukemia (AML) exhibits extensive inter- and intra-patient antigenic heterogeneity, representing a major obstacle for chimeric antigen receptor (CAR)-based therapies. Cellular platforms that combine potent direct cytotoxicity with the ability to engage endogenous immune responses may help overcome this limitation. Invariant natural killer T (iNKT) cells are particularly attractive for allogeneic immunotherapy because of their lack of alloreactivity and their capacity to promote cross-priming of conventional T cells. To exploit these properties in AML, we generated CD33-directed CAR iNKT cells and demonstrated direct antitumor activity against CD33-expressing AML cells both in vitro and in vivo. Using an in vitro mixed-tumor model composed of parental CD33-expressing and CD33-knockout MOLM-14 cells we show that CD33-CAR iNKT cells efficiently eliminated CD33-positive leukemia cells but did not directly control the growth of CD33-knockout cells. However, the addition of conventional T cells, particularly CD8 T cells, together with CD33-CAR iNKT cells resulted in robust T-cell activation and subsequent control of CD33-knockout MOLM-14 cells. Importantly, CD33-CAR iNKT cells induced marked phenotypic changes in antigen-negative leukemia cells, including upregulation of HLA class I and class II molecules, suggesting increased immunogenicity. Finally, we recapitulated both the antitumor and immunomodulatory effects of CD33-CAR iNKT cells in primary bone marrow samples from patients with newly diagnosed AML. Collectively, these findings show that CD33-CAR iNKT cells can promote CD8 T-cell immunity against AML and support a therapeutic strategy capable of extending antitumor activity beyond the targeted antigen, thereby helping to overcome antigenic heterogeneity.

papers.title: CNS-derived SerpinA3n restricts pathogenesis during WNV encephalitis via suppression of inflammatory protease activity
papers.abstract: Proteolytic activity is integral to host immune defense, yet little is known about how proteolytic homeostasis is maintained in the central nervous system (CNS) during viral infection. Here, we investigated roles for the serine protease inhibitor SerpinA3n in promoting host protection during West Nile virus (WNV) encephalitis. WNV neuroinvasion was accompanied by widespread induction of serpin expression, including SerpinA3n. Pharmacological inhibition of SerpinA3n within the CNS, but not in the periphery, exacerbated mortality, whereas CNS supplementation with recombinant SerpinA3n improved survival, preserved blood-brain barrier (BBB) integrity, and reduced proteolytic activity and leukocyte accumulation without altering CNS viral burden. Using cell-type-specific genetic deletion, we identified astrocytes and neurons as major sources of SerpinA3n in the infected CNS. Loss of SerpinA3n from either cell population increased mortality, BBB permeability, and gelatinase/collagenase activity. However, loss of neuronal, but not astrocytic, SerpinA3n exacerbated leukocyte accumulation and antigen-presenting cell activation, suggesting that the cellular context of SerpinA3n production influences its immunoregulatory functions. Both astrocyte- and neuron-derived SerpinA3n restrained granzyme B activity in the infected CNS, and neutralization of granzyme B reversed the excess mortality associated with pharmacological inhibition of SerpinA3n. Together, these findings identify serpin-mediated regulation of inflammatory protease activity as a mechanism of host protection during viral encephalitis and establish both neurons and astrocytes as important contributors to the maintenance of proteolytic homeostasis in the inflamed CNS.

papers.title: Stk11 deficiency promotes tumor CXCL16 secretion and a CXCL16-dependent expansion of Aregpos CXCR6pos Vγ6 γδT17 in lung cancer
papers.abstract: IL-17-producing gamma delta ({gamma}{delta}T17) T cells can promote tumor growth and metastasis. How the tumor microenvironment controls the activation, expansion, and function of {gamma}{delta}T17 in different cancers remains unclear. Using an autochthonous model of KrasG12D/Stk11-driven lung adenocarcinoma coupled with scRNAseq and V(D)J profiling, we found that KrasG12DStk11-loss tumors induced a rapid expansion of lung CXCR6+ V{gamma}4 and amphiregulin-expressing CXCR6+ V{gamma}6{gamma}{delta}T17 cells. Single-cell immune profiling of the KrasG12DStk11-loss tumors revealed a prominent Krt8+ alveolar epithelial cell (KAC) tumor subtype enriched in a number of immune-relevant genes, including Cxcl16 and its sheddase Adam10, and in vitro culture revealed that KACs, but not their normal epithelial cell counterparts, secreted CXCL16. Finally, we found that in vivo blockade of CXCL16 inhibited the expansion of lung V{gamma}6+ {gamma}{delta}T17 in response to KrasG12DStk11-loss tumors. Together, these data suggest that Stk11 loss promotes a CXCL16-secreting Krt8+ KAC tumor subtype, and that CXCL16-CXCR6 interactions are necessary to drive the expansion of pro-tumor {gamma}{delta}T17 cells in lung cancer.

papers.title: Neutrophil lectin-like oxidized low-density lipoprotein receptor (LOX-1) limits inflammatory injury during bacterial pneumonia.
papers.abstract: Pneumonia is an inflammatory condition that is caused by myriad microorganisms, necessitating broadly applicable therapeutics. Yet, host determinants of pneumonia severity remain poorly understood, demanding a more complete understanding of the cells and signals that control tissue homeostasis. Our group previously showed that the class E scavenger receptor lectin-like oxidized low-density lipoprotein receptor-1 (LOX-1) limits pneumonia-induced lung injury without affecting bacterial clearance, contrasting its well-established injurious effects in the setting of atherosclerosis. These findings indicate that location and cell type are key determinants of LOX-1 function, but cell-specific sources of LOX-1-mediated lung protection are unknown. Here, we show that a portion of lung-recruited neutrophils are stimulated to express LOX-1 upon entry into the airspaces of humans and mice during pneumonia. Neutrophil LOX-1 expression correlates with higher levels of chemokine and scavenger receptors, reactive oxygen species, and apoptotic markers that likely influence their phenotype and potentially those of neighboring cells. To determine whether neutrophil LOX-1 contributes to LOX-1-dependent tissue protection, we generated neutrophil-specific LOX-1 knockout mice (LOX-1{Delta}MRP8) and assessed their acute response to two models of bacterial pneumonia, Escherichia coli and Streptococcus pneumoniae. Elevated metrics of inflammation were detected in LOX-1{Delta}MRP8 mice following both challenges, including reduced survival during E. coli infection, without changes in bacterial clearance. Finally, deletion of LOX-1 on neutrophils resulted in modifications to the neutrophil phenotype that may contribute to increased recruitment and inflammatory potential in the airspace. Taken together, LOX-1 is a scavenger receptor that is induced on a population of neutrophils in the pneumonic airspaces, taming further neutrophilic inflammation to limit immunopathology.

papers.title: Human hematopoietic development during the first year of life and its remodeling by neonatal Bacillus Calmette-Guerin vaccination
papers.abstract: Hematopoiesis and immune development are well defined in adults but remain poorly understood in early life, despite the neonatal period being critical for immune maturation. We map hematopoietic and immune programs across the first year of human life using single-nucleus epigenomic and transcriptomic profiling of circulating hematopoietic stem and progenitor cells (cHSPCs), including Bacillus Calmette-Guerin (BCG) vaccinated infants to illustrate a controlled immune challenge. BCG-naive infants displayed heightened myeloid activation through 3 months of age, followed by an interferon-enriched HSPC program at 13 months. BCG vaccination induced earlier interferon responses in HSPCs and dampened inflammatory programs in myeloid cells. These findings define the landscape of early-life human hematopoiesis and provide mechanistic insight into the heterologous protection associated with neonatal BCG vaccination.

papers.title: The IFN-γ Paradox: Mechanistic Modeling Uncouples Cytokine Abundance from Influenza Pathogenesis
papers.abstract: IFN-{gamma} has both pathogenic and protective roles during influenza infection, yet its value as a biomarker remains unclear because both increased and decreased levels associate with greater severity. To resolve this, we developed a mechanistic mathematical model of IFN-{gamma} and IFN-{gamma}-producing cell kinetics. The model was calibrated using murine data and validated against immune perturbation experiments, murine transcriptomics, human influenza challenge, and critically ill patient data. Personalizing the model with human challenge data quantified interindividual heterogeneity and generating cohorts of virtual patients with varying degrees of severity predicted unmeasured dynamics and was validated with transcriptomic and proteomic data from critically ill patients. Although severe disease was associated with greater receptor-mediated IFN-{gamma} uptake despite comparable production in non-ICU and ICU patients, early innate IFN-{gamma} signaling was a stronger determinant. These findings explain divergent IFN-{gamma} responses and establish a mechanistic framework for interpreting cytokine measurements.

papers.title: Alternative splicing links sex to neutrophil inflammatory vulnerability
papers.abstract: Mammalian females generally live longer than males, yet the immunological drivers governing sex-biased inflammatory mortality remain unclear. Neutrophils, among conserved immune cells across species, exhibit marked sex differences in inflammatory and age-related diseases. We identified conserved male-biased CD11b expression in resting neutrophils of wild-type mice, Rag2 KO mice, and in human cohorts. Male neutrophils selectively displayed CD11b-dependent transendothelial migration. During tissue inflammation in our mouse model deficient in -Klotho (Kl) combined with Rag2 KO lymphocyte depletion (dKO), males showed higher mortality and more severe pulmonary pathology correlated with increased infiltrating neutrophils in the lung. The neutrophil accumulation directly accounted for heightened IL-1{beta} expression in males despite equivalent per-cell cytokine expression across sexes. Transcriptomic analysis of neutrophils revealed profound sex-biased alternative splicing enriched in Toll-like receptor (TLR) cascades, alongside hormone-responsive regulation of integrin {beta}2 (Itgb2) isoform usage, implicating alternative splicing in neutrophils represents male vulnerability to tissue inflammation.

papers.title: Intravenous BCG Elicits a Sustained Myeloid IFNG Response Signature Associated with Early TB Control
papers.abstract: Bacille Calmette-Guerin (BCG) administered intravenously (IV) to rhesus macaques can prevent pulmonary tuberculosis (TB) infection. To establish transcriptional correlates of protection, we generated longitudinal CITE-Seq data across blood and lung after IV BCG in macaques and compared it to clinically approved intradermal (ID) BCG. We define an interferon gamma (IFNG) response signature in alveolar macrophages (AMs) comprising 61 genes with diverging expression between IV and ID BCG from 4 to 16 weeks after vaccination that was also enriched in AMs early after TB challenge. The signature was recapitulated in blood monocytes (IV vs. ID) and associated with protection in an independent cohort of IV BCG-vaccinated macaques. Cell-cell communication analysis inferred increased ligand-receptor interactions in the airway after IV BCG, including those between multiple IFNG-producing T cell subsets and AMs. The sustained IFNG response signature in AMs after IV BCG provides a new correlate and potential mechanism of early TB control informing future vaccine design.

papers.title: Cholesterol and high concentration serum cooperatively enhance canine CAR T cell transduction and expansion
papers.abstract: Chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) T cell immunotherapy is emerging as a promising adjunct treatment option for refractory canine cancers. Unfortunately, clinical trials thus far have failed to meaningfully reduce tumor burden, highlighting the need for improved CAR T cell manufacturing strategies. Effective autologous therapy requires highly viable, efficiently transduced T cells capable of robust expansion, sustained CAR expression, and long-term persistence. Although these parameters have been extensively investigated in humans, comparable optimization in canine systems remains limited. Here, we evaluated culture conditions to improve canine T cell expansion, memory differentiation, and retroviral transduction efficiency. We demonstrated IL-2 supplementation supported superior cellular expansion and preservation of less-differentiated memory phenotypes compared to IL-7 with IL-15. Additionally, we found that increasing cell density during shorter stimulation periods improved expansion while also driving better T cell transduction rates. We discovered that the addition of cholesterol and high-concentration fetal bovine serum (FBS) to media during the transduction period reliably and markedly enhanced transduction efficiency following a single round of retroviral transduction, even at elevated temperatures that would otherwise impair transduction efficiency. This enhancement was observed with both GALV- and RD114-pseudotyped retroviruses and was accompanied by a marked improvement in cellular expansion without driving terminal differentiation of T cell subsets that are prone to exhaustion in vivo. Collectively, these findings identify practical strategies to improve canine CAR T-cell manufacturing and advance the development of clinically viable CAR T cells for canine cancer treatment.

papers.title: Single cell mapping reveals phenotypic, immunometabolic and functional heterogeneity among age-associated B cells in systemic lupus erythematosus and aging
papers.abstract: Abstract/Summary Introduction: Age-associated B cells (ABCs) comprise an antigen-experienced memory B-cell population that expands during aging but has also been implicated in autoimmune diseases, particularly systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE). Cell immunometabolism has emerged as a key determinant of immune-cell function, linking metabolic adaptation to both protective and maladaptive immunity or pathological inflammation, thereby providing a platform for therapeutic intervention. This study aims to comprehensively profile the functional alterations that accommodate ABC expansion, emphasizing metabolic reprogramming within the B-cell compartment in SLE, particularly with regard to ABCs, in order to identify niche metabolic pathways utilized by ABCs that may represent useful therapeutic targets. Methods: An exploratory analysis was conducted using publicly available single-cell RNA sequencing datasets to phenotypically and functionally characterize ABC populations in patients with SLE and lupus-prone MRL.lpr mice, using a broad array of community tools. We further conducted SCENITH-based metabolic profiling to assess metabolic differences among splenic follicular (FO), marginal zone (MZ) and CD21-CD23- double negative (DN) B cells, in the murine SLE-like MRL.lpr model, in which we tested the ability of B cell subsets to generate protein output, following exposure to specific metabolic inhibitors (2-deoxyglucose and oligomycin). In addition, we cross-examined CD21-CD23- DN B cells in the native context of aging by employing flow cytometry-based analyses of their redox status (NADH/FAD autofluorescence) and mitochondrial function (MitoTracker and TMRE staining) to investigate age-associated metabolic programming. Results: Single-cell transcriptomic analyses revealed substantial immunophenotypic and metabolic heterogeneity within the ABC compartment in SLE. Subclustering of ABCs revealed three separate and distinct ABC subsets, encompassing CD68 ABCs, NKG7 ABCs, and AREG ABCs, differing in their respecrive transcriptional, functional, and immunometabolic signatures. The CD68 ABC subset demonstrated signs of enhanced cytotoxicity, phagocytosis, lysosomal activity, and increased antigen-processing capabilities. The CD68 and NKG7 ABC populations exhibited increased inflammatory pathway activity, including pattern-recognition receptor signalling and NLRP3 inflammasome-associated activity, while the AREG ABC subset displayed signs of senescence, moderation, exhaustion, or anergy. hdWGCNA identified transcriptional modules associated with acetyltransferase activity, suggesting a potential link between metabolic reprogramming and epigenetic remodelling through epimetabolite availability, in particular acetyl-CoA. ABCs demonstrated, in general, coordinated amplification of glycolysis, oxidative phosphorylation, and lipid utilization, with substantial intragroup metabolic heterogeneity among the three ABC subsets. The CD68 ABCs emerged as the most hypermetabolic subset. In parallel, SCENITH-based metabolic comparison of CD21-CD23- DN B cells between mildly diseased male and severely diseased female MRL.lpr mice revealed increased utilization of alternative non-glucose substrates and enhanced glycolytic activity, but reduced overall protein synthesis capacity, indicating altered allocation of metabolic resources. Further interpretation of the transcriptomic analysis suggests that proteasomal activity could explain the lower protein levels in female MRL.lpr mice, as measured by SCENITH. In addition, in silico drug prediction pointed towards statins and proteasome inhibitors as potentially useful pharmacological agents for blocking cholesterol metabolism and protein degradation, respectively. Finally, the analysis of aged mice also revealed metabolic and redox alterations in ABC-enriched CD21-CD23- DN B cells under physiological aging conditions. Conclusions: Human ABCs appear to comprise a heterogeneous constellation of various subsets possessing different functional properties, as well as different pro-inflammatory or immunoregulatory statuses. ABCs exhibit a distinct hypermetabolic state associated with lupus-related immune dysregulation, but also with aging, in line with previous reports. However, as the disease manifests and progresses, protein production appears to be dampened, which could be attributed to ribosomal problems or proteasome-mediated protein degradation. Metabolic reprogramming is accompanied by enhanced phagocytic and lysosomal programs, which may facilitate the uptake of self-material and contribute to autoreactive immune responses, in particular anti-nuclear autoantibody production. Increased OXPHOS activity may accommodate epigenetic reprogramming towards the atypical memory phenotype displayed by ABCs. Identification of ABC-specific metabolic dependencies may provide opportunities for therapeutic intervention, with lipid consumption being of particular interest. These findings support further investigation of metabolic modulators, including HMG-CoA reductase inhibitors and proteasome-targeting strategies, to limit their pathogenic activity in SLE by exploiting their niche metabolic vulnerabilities, in particular their hypermetabolic state and proteostatic stress.

papers.title: Nsg2 deficiency attenuates intestinal inflammation and colitis-associated tumorigenesis through microbiome-dependent metabolic remodeling
papers.abstract: Background & Aims Neuron-Specific Gene 2 (NSG2) is a neuronally expressed protein that facilitates excitatory synaptic transmission through the regulation of AMPA receptor trafficking. While its function has been characterized in the central nervous system, whether NSG2 plays a role in enteric neuronal signaling and intestinal pathology has yet to be explored. We therefore investigated whether Nsg2 deficiency modulates intestinal inflammation and tumorigenesis through gut microbiome-dependent mechanisms. Methods Dextran sulfate sodium (DSS)-induced colitis and azoxymethane/DSS-induced colitis-associated cancer (DSS-CAC) models were established in Nsg2-/- and wild-type (WT) mice. Disease severity was evaluated using the disease activity index (DAI), histopathological scoring, and tumor burden assessment. To investigate the potential contribution of the gut microbiota to genotype-associated phenotypes, WT and Nsg2-/- mice were co-housed for six weeks before disease induction. Gut microbial composition and predicted functional pathways were analyzed using 16S rRNA gene sequencing (V3-V4 region) and PICRUSt2, respectively. Results Separately housed Nsg2-/- mice exhibited significantly attenuated DSS-induced colitis, with reduced body weight loss, lower DAI scores, and preserved colonic architecture. In the DSS-CAC model, Nsg2-/- mice developed significantly fewer and smaller tumors with suppressed Wnt/beta-catenin signaling. Under co-housing conditions, no statistically significant differences in colitis severity or tumor burden were detected between genotypes, supporting a possible contribution of the gut microbiota to the phenotypes observed in separately housed mice. 16S rRNA sequencing identified distinct microbial communities in Nsg2-/- mice, characterized by greater alpha diversity and enrichment of protective taxa, including Butyricicoccus and Lachnospiraceae. Functional profiling predicted enrichment of methane metabolism, porphyrin biosynthesis, and one-carbon metabolism pathways. Conclusions Nsg2 deficiency confers protection against intestinal inflammation and colitis-associated tumorigenesis, accompanied by alterations in gut microbial composition and suppression of Wnt/beta-catenin signaling. These findings identify NSG2 as a novel modulator at the intersection of enteric neuronal signaling, gut microbiota, and mucosal immunity, positioning it as a potential therapeutic target for IBD and inflammation-driven colorectal cancer.

papers.title: Fibronectin binding and non-canonical transcription factor signature distinguishes lung and bone marrow megakaryocytes
papers.abstract: Recent evidence has demonstrated the unique morphology and function of lung megakaryocytes (MKs), yet the source of the differences between lung and bone marrow (BM) MKs remains unclear. While BM MKs are large, polyploid, BM-resident cells primarily known as platelet producing cells, lung MKs are smaller, less polyploid, and known for immunomodulation. To better understand the factors underlying the differences in lung and BM MKs, we developed a flow cytometry method for precise characterization and isolation of MKs using leukocyte exclusion and examination of hematopoietic and canonical MK markers. When MK-leukocyte aggregates are excluded, a single femur+tibia contains approximately 1,493 MKs and a single lung contains approximately 4,541 MKs. Enrichment via positive selection efficiently removes unwanted cells, increasing the percentage of MKs amongst live lung cells by 10.29-fold and the percentage of MKs amongst live BM cells by 29.09-fold. Sorted MKs were viable and spread onto fibrinogen. Gene expression analysis demonstrated that lung MKs increase immune pathway gene expression, including TNFRSF1B. Transcription factor (TF) and cell cycle gene expression decreased in lung MKs compared to BM MKs, including reduced expression of GATA1 and CDC6, possibly explaining observations of low ploidy and size in lung MKs, while expression of the TF ETS2 increased. Lung MKs also express increased ITGA4 compared to BM MKs, abundant surface integrin 4 protein, and increased surface integrin {beta}7 protein compared to BM MKs. Additionally, lung MKs bind significantly more fibronectin ex vivo then BM MKs. These data demonstrate for the first time that lung MKs have a unique TF signature and suggests integrin 4{beta}7 as a relevant receptor for lung MK function.

papers.title: mRNA-1273.262 and mRNA-1283.262 Vaccines Expressing XFG Antigens Neutralize Relevant Circulating Variants
papers.abstract: SARS-CoV-2 continues to circulate and causes substantial disease burden as an endemic respiratory pathogen. Vaccination is a key public health measure to ameliorate the effects of COVID-19 disease but requires annual update to match strains that are circulating. Monitoring of circulating virus and characterization of matched candidate vaccines helps to inform which antigens will provide the greatest benefit to public well-being. The 2026-2027 season will leverage XFG as the variant of interest for vaccine production and in vitro and in vivo data was generated preclinically to support this selection. XFG variant vaccines express well in mRNA format as both full-length spike and linked subdomain antigen formats. Animals immunized with these vaccines elicit robust neutralizing responses to relevant JN.1-family virus variants in both primary series and booster models. In future seasons, robust epidemiologically monitoring including viral genome sequencing will improve early detection of relevant variants and subsequent preparation of vaccine antigens.

papers.title: Single-cell T cell receptor sequencing deciphers αβ- and γδ-T cell responses in neuroblastoma
authors: A. F. W. van der Steeg
papers.abstract: High-risk neuroblastoma is a pediatric tumor with poor survival rates and low MHC-I expression. The cellular determinants of anti-tumor immunity remain poorly defined, limiting development of targeted immunotherapies. We generated a single-cell atlas integrating transcriptomic and {beta}/{gamma}{delta} T cell receptor (TCR) sequencing of >150,000 T cells from tumor and blood of 10 patients throughout treatment. Fractions of CD8+ and CD4+ T cells are clonally expanded and activated, with tumor-specific expansion among CD4+ cells. Transcriptomic evidence of tumor-reactivity is more pronounced in CD4+ than CD8+ T cells. Moreover, V{delta}1+ {gamma}{delta}T cells are enriched, displaying TCR engagement. Functional screening confirmed reactivity of selected {gamma}{delta}TCRs and, remarkably, a small fraction of CD8+ {beta}TCRs. Subset-specific inhibitory receptors, including CTLA4, FCRL6, and KIRs, may serve as targets for tailored immunotherapies. Together, we identify distinct {beta}- and {gamma}{delta}T cell responses despite low MHC-I, and provide a comprehensive resource for deciphering pediatric immunity against MHC-Ilow tumors.

papers.title: Lipin-1-cardiolipin axis sustains mitochondrial respiration and efferocytosis in macrophages
papers.abstract: Defective macrophage clearance of apoptotic cells contributes to persistent inflammation and cardiometabolic disease. Efferocytosis requires mitochondrial oxidative metabolism, but how macrophages maintain respiratory capacity during resolution remains unclear. Here, we show that lipin-1 supports efferocytosis through a cardiolipin-associated mitochondrial program. In IL-4-stimulated macrophages, lipin-1 deficiency reduced cardiolipin abundance and selectively lowered the abundance of inner mitochondrial membrane proteins, including respiratory-chain components, consistent with decreased mitochondrial respiratory capacity. These defects occurred without broad suppression of canonical metabolic transcriptional programs, and experimentally altering mitochondrial morphology failed to reproduce or rescue the functional phenotype. Disrupting cardiolipin synthesis impaired efferocytosis, whereas the cardiolipin-interacting peptide SS-31 improved mitochondrial respiration and apoptotic-cell clearance in lipin-1-deficient macrophages. Systemic SS-31 treatment also reduced apoptotic-cell accumulation after dexamethasone-induced thymic injury. Together, these findings implicate cardiolipin homeostasis in lipin-1-dependent macrophage bioenergetics and efferocytosis, identifying a potentially actionable pathway while leaving the mechanism connecting lipin-1 to cardiolipin abundance unresolved.

papers.title: Tnfrsf13b Variants Enhance IgG-Mediated Complement Responses to Promote Bacterial Clearance
papers.abstract: RSF13B encodes the TACI receptor, necessary for differentiation of B cells into plasma cells. TNFRSF13B is highly polymorphic, yet common non-synonymous variants including those that impair the receptor structure and/or signaling are retained in the population. Here we show that mice carrying the Tnfrsf13b A144E variant, the murine homolog of the human TNFRSF13B A181E variant associated with common variable immunodeficiency, effectively clear host-adapted Citrobacter rodentium (a murine model of pathogenic E. coli infection) despite nine-fold decreased bacteria-specific IgG compared to WT mice. IgG from Tnfrsf13b mutant mice exhibited reduced sialic acid, terminal galactose, fucose, and showed enhanced complement effector functions, including greater C1q binding and membrane attack complex (C5b) deposition. Results show that some Tnfrsf13b variants enhance complement-dependent antibody effector function, thereby identifying TACI as a regulator of IgG effector properties and providing a potential explanation for the evolutionary persistence of TNFRSF13B mutations.

papers.title: Longitudinal multiomics analysis in blood from individuals before and after HIV acquisition
papers.abstract: A comprehensive understanding of cellular immunity is essential for controlling viral infections, yet individual and coordinated immune responses continue to pose significant challenges in HIV cure research. Recent advances in single-cell and multiomics technologies provide powerful tools to dissect intricate multicellular behaviors and identify novel therapeutic targets. Direct characterization of HIV-induced immune alterations is challenging because matched samples obtained before HIV acquisition are rare. To better understand individual and coordinated cellular immune responses relevant to HIV cure research, we integrated single-nucleus chromatin-accessibility and transcriptomic profiling of 150,060 PBMCs with plasma metabolome, lipidome and soluble immune-profiling from five individuals before HIV acquisition, during early infection and after at least six months of suppressive antiretroviral therapy (ART). HIV acquisition expanded activated CD8 T and proliferating NK/CD8 T cells and induced cell-type-specific chromatin and transcriptional changes enriched for interferon, inflammatory and TNF-NF-{kappa}B programs, many persisting during ART. Multiome sequencing detected 32 HIV-positive cells which were associated with increased expression of IFI44L during early infection and ATAD3A after ART. Plasma IP-10 increased transiently, whereas eight energy- or amino-acid-related metabolites showed nominal decreases persisting after ART. These paired observations distinguish transient inflammatory responses from persistent molecular and metabolic perturbations after HIV acquisition.

papers.title: Host glycans trap bacterial lectins to trigger NLRP3 inflammasome activation
papers.abstract: Pseudomonas aeruginosa poses a severe threat to immunocompromised patients through its multifaceted virulence arsenal. Although diverse bacterial components activate the NLRP3 inflammasome, the precise molecular triggers driving this process remain largely elusive. Here, we reveal that host surface glycans effectively trap the P. aeruginosa lectins LecA and LecB, initiating carbohydrate-dependent inflammasome activation. This lectin-mediated cascade exhibits striking host-species and cell-type specificity. The L-fucose-specific LecB activates human blood monocytes and THP-1 cells, where glycosylated {beta}1-integrin contributes to signal transduction, whereas the D-galactose-specific LecA is more potent in murine bone marrow-derived macrophages and dendritic cells. This mechanism requires potassium efflux and displays cell-specific sensitivity to reactive oxygen species. Infection with live bacteria recapitulates the lectin-mediated inflammasome response. Collectively, our findings unveil an unexpected role for host glycans as critical, previously overlooked checkpoints gating P. aeruginosa-driven inflammation, offering fresh insights into host-pathogen dynamics and exposing novel therapeutic targets.
